items.title: 15.4 How to check the purity of the product

source_refs.note: Topic 15.4, printed page 332. The exercise (pages 333-335) is not reproduced.

blocks.text: Different methods purify compounds that are liquids or solids under normal conditions. Liquids are generally purified by distillation at normal pressure or under vacuum, and their purity is checked by comparing their boiling points with the literature values.

Aspirin, an important analgesic and antipyretic, is prepared by reacting salicylic acid with excess acetic anhydride in the presence of a few drops of concentrated sulfuric acid. After the reaction, water is added to precipitate the aspirin, the mixture is filtered to give the crude product, and it is crystallized from water as the polar solvent.

items: The aspirin may be mixed with unreacted salicylic acid. Its melting point is determined: if the product melts sharply, at exactly 136 degrees C, it is pure; if it melts over a range of temperature it is impure.
A mixed melting point: the product is mixed with a pure sample of aspirin and the melting point determined; if it is still sharp the product is pure.
Paper chromatography of the sample alongside pure aspirin and pure salicylic acid, matching the Rf values.

blocks.text: How does the melting point indicate purity, and how would you check a laboratory sample of glucosazone?
